title: Can I plant a rose where another rose grew?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources disagree on how real replant disease is and what to do about it (C-4). No comparison of remedies in home gardens was found (R-3). The amount of soil to replace differs, including between two pages of the same body. That the cause is not established (AF-12), and that the problem can persist for at least nine years (AF-14, one source, not said of roses), are not used.

content.heading: Can I plant a rose where another rose grew?

items.text: A new rose planted where a rose grew before may struggle to establish and may grow poorly. This is called replant disease.

If you plant in the same spot, swap the soil in the planting hole for fresh soil from another part of the garden. Sources differ on how much to take out: from two buckets of soil, along with the old rose's roots, to a hole 45 to 60 cm (18 to 24 inches) across and 30 to 45 cm (12 to 18 inches) deep. One source gives planting somewhere else as another option.

Experts disagree about replant disease. Several advise replacing the soil. One rose specialist calls that the old method and instead adds compost or well-rotted manure and treats the new rose with mycorrhizal fungi. That source reports that opinion is divided on whether the problem is real.
I couldn't find a comparison of which remedy for replant disease works best in a home garden. A local rose society is the place to ask.
